Footman
FOOT-man
noun
From foot and man — a soldier who serves on foot, as distinguished from the horseman and the charioteer. It renders the Hebrew raglī, “one on foot,” and in one place the royal runners or guardsmen.

Biblical Definition

A footman in the Authorized Version is not a servant in livery but an infantryman — the soldier who marches and fights on his own two feet, counted by the hundred thousand in Israel's musters. Moses reckons the nation at “six hundred thousand footmen” (Num 11:21); Israel assembles “four hundred thousand footmen that drew sword” (Jdg 20:2); and when the ark was taken there fell of Israel “thirty thousand footmen” (1Sa 4:10). The footman is the common man of the host, the rank the LORD most often used and most often thinned. But the word receives its enduring weight from a single question the LORD puts to a weary prophet. Jeremiah had complained of the men of Anathoth who sought his life, and the answer he got was not comfort but a harder charge: “If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?” (Jer 12:5). Here is the whole doctrine of Christian endurance in one verse. The footrace is the light trial; the horses and the flooded Jordan are what is coming. God does not answer weariness by lowering the course — He answers it by strengthening the runner for a heavier one.

Webster 1828 Definition

A soldier who marches and fights on foot; an infantryman, as opposed to a horseman.

FOOTMAN, a soldier who marches and fights on foot; foot-soldier; infantry.

From foot and man; Hebrew raglī, one who goes on foot.

In the Authorized Version it is a military word, not the later English sense of a liveried servant.

Israel's musters are counted in footmen — six hundred thousand at Sinai (Num 11:21).

Jeremiah is asked how he will contend with horses if footmen have wearied him (Jer 12:5).

Key Scripture

Jer 12:5 — "If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?"

Num 11:21 — "And Moses said, The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month."

Jdg 20:2 — "And the chief of all the people, even of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, four hundred thousand footmen that drew sword."

1Sa 4:10 — "And the Philistines fought, and Israel was smitten, and they fled every man into his tent: and there was a very great slaughter; for there fell of Israel thirty thousand footmen."

Modern Corruption

An honest old word for the infantryman; the corruption is an age that treats weariness as proof that the calling was wrong.

expand to see more

The therapeutic instinct of our day answers Jeremiah's complaint the way God did not. Told that the footmen have wearied him, the modern counsellor lightens the load, renames the calling a poor fit, and treats fatigue itself as the verdict on a man's vocation. The LORD's answer runs the opposite way. He does not deny that the prophet is tired, and He does not scold him for saying so; He tells him plainly that horses are coming, and that the swelling of Jordan lies beyond the land of peace. That is not cruelty. It is the honesty of a Commander who intends His man to survive the real war, and who knows that a soldier flattered in the easy season is a soldier destroyed in the hard one.

The recovery is the biblical doctrine of endurance: strength is given for the race actually set, and it is given in the running, not before it. “They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength… they shall run, and not be weary” (Isa 40:31), and the runner is bidden to “run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus” (Heb 12:1–2). Note where the eyes go. Not to the length of the course and not inward to the state of one's own reserves, but to the Forerunner who ran the whole distance, contended with horses, went down into the swelling of Jordan, and came up on the other side. Jeremiah kept his post for forty more years on that answer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Footman = the infantryman, the soldier on foot; Hebrew raglī, “one on foot.”

expand to see more

Footman — foot + man; the soldier who marches and fights afoot.

Hebrew raglī, from regel, the foot; opposed to the horseman and charioteer.

Not the liveried house-servant of later English — always a man of war in the AV.

Israel's armies are numbered in footmen (Num 11:21; Jdg 20:2; 1Sa 4:10).

Jer 12:5 makes the footrace the emblem of the lighter trial that trains a man for the heavier.

Usage

"If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee — then horses are coming."

"God answers weariness not by shortening the course but by strengthening the runner."

"A footman is the common man of the host — the rank God most often uses."
